speakwise.title: SpeakWise — Child Speech Recognition Research
subtitles: Building a speech recognizer that keeps the details of what a child says
Researcher & Developer · Independent Speech Research · Patent Pending

paragraphs: A friend and my younger brother had faced speech difficulties since childhood. I built a prototype combining recognition, adjustable correction, and voice cloning, hoping to help. Their feedback taught me that sounding smoother was not necessarily what they wanted.

That changed the question I was asking. Phase 1 explored giving speakers control over edits while keeping their own voice. In Phase 2, I focused on an earlier step: faithfully recognizing the words, repetitions, and fillers a child actually said.
I developed the system and adapted the recognizer independently. SpeakWise remains a research project; its results do not establish clinical effectiveness.

0.title: Prototype: Recognition → Editing → Synthesis
0.intro: The early prototype explored how information changes across a three-stage pipeline:

items.title: Transcribe the speech
items.body: Whisper turns audio into text. I keep the input available because a recognizer can miss words, repetitions, or fillers.

items.title: Choose how much to edit
items.body: An LLM proposes edits, with a correction setting that adjusts how much changes. The original transcript stays separate from the suggestion.

items.title: Hear the revised version
items.body: XTTS uses voice cloning to read the edited text in a version of the speaker’s own voice. The aim is to offer help without replacing their voice.

paragraphs: I added a correction setting, λ, so the amount of editing could vary. The speaker can compare the proposed revision with the original rather than receive one fixed level of correction.
1.title: A Control Over How Much Changes

paragraphs: Speech arrives a little at a time. Responding quickly leaves less context; waiting can interrupt a conversation. I still need to measure that trade-off alongside recognition and editing errors.
2.title: Responding Before the Sentence Is Finished

paragraphs: Filed August 23, 2026, with me as first-named inventor. The application covers controllable speech repair, preserving the original utterance, and synthesizing revisions in the speaker’s own voice. It is patent pending.
1.title: Scope and Status

items.body: Systems and Methods for Controllable, Evidence-Preserving Speech Repair with Identity-Preserving Synthesis
items.label: Title

items.body: August 23, 2026
items.label: Filing / Receipt Date

items.body: Ethan Li
items.label: First-named inventor

Interdisciplinary Linguistics Component.heading: What Gets Kept in a Transcript?

0.intro: The project has led me to think about three questions:

items.label: Keeping the details
items.body: A repetition or filler is something we can look for in a transcript. Keeping it gives someone a chance to examine it later.

items.label: Words and meaning
items.body: An edited sentence may read more smoothly but change the original wording. I keep the transcript and the suggested edit separate.

items.label: The bigger picture
items.body: Counting word errors cannot tell me everything about whether an edit kept the speaker’s meaning. That still needs context and human judgment.

paragraphs: Keeping a repeated word leaves someone a choice about what to do with it. Understanding why it was repeated still needs context. That distinction drew me toward studying language as well as building speech tools.

1.title: What a Useful Speech Tool Must Make Visible
1.intro: Producing fluent text is only one part of the problem:
items: Distinguish the recorded utterance, the recognizer’s transcript, and any proposed rewrite.
Make recognition and editing failures inspectable instead of presenting a polished result as ground truth.
Keep identifiable recordings and child-related data private; public examples require appropriate permission.

paragraphs: The next step is to test how the recognizer works inside the larger application. That means checking speed, privacy, editing quality, and whether users can see and control changes to their speech.
2.title: Application Boundaries

columns.heading: Speech Models
items: Phase 1: Whisper transcription, LLM editing, XTTS voice synthesis
Phase 2: wav2vec 2.0 with CTC
Speaker-separated evaluation; word errors and repetition/filler recall

columns.heading: Application
items: Python backend
WebSocket streaming prototype
Docker deployment

Expected Outcomes & Scholarly Contributi.heading: Questions That Came Out of the Prototype

items.label: Access
items.body: Could a practice interface be easier to reach and use? Accessibility is a design goal, not a demonstrated treatment outcome.

items.label: Agency
items.body: Can a person inspect or reject a revision rather than have their speech silently replaced?

items.label: Evaluation
items.body: How should transcription quality, editing quality, and usefulness of feedback be evaluated separately?

1.title: Questions I Had to Think About
1.intro: Building it raised a few related questions:

items.label: Speech processing
items.body: Check transcription errors and whether repetitions and fillers are kept.

items.label: What the transcript keeps
items.body: Keep a record of what was said separate from an edited version.

items.label: Information quality
items.body: Ask what is lost between audio, text, and synthesized output, and make those losses visible.

items.label: Human-computer interaction
items.body: Treat control over editing and access to the original as interface questions.

paragraphs: SpeakWise received Honorable Mention at the Dallas Regional Science & Engineering Fair and first place at the Highland Park High School SciTech Fair, with a $3,000 award. These recognized the earlier speech-repair prototype.
2.title: Science Fair Recognition

paragraphs: For Phase 2, I adapted wav2vec 2.0 with CTC to children’s speech. The study used 116.0 hours of training audio from 1,738 children (64,941 utterances), then evaluated 17,306 utterances from 434 children kept separate from training.

The manuscript reports a 21.74% word error rate and 69.1% recall for marked fillers and immediate whole-word repetitions. Word error rate counts replaced, missing, and added words; recall measures how many of the marked details the transcript kept. Neither score measures a child’s fluency or a therapy outcome.

I also adapted the recognizer with 3.88 hours of preschool speech from 36 children. On 1,293 paired validation utterances from nine unseen four-year-olds, word error rate fell from 79.31% to 68.95%. Errors remained high, and the small group limits what I can conclude.

These are results reported in the Phase 2 manuscript summarized in the poster above. My sole-authored paper was accepted for presentation at the IEEE BigData 2026 High School Symposium, scheduled for December 17, 2026, in Phoenix.

items.label: Transcription errors
items.body: I used word error rate to count replaced, missing, and added words. It measures transcription mistakes, not how fluently a child speaks.

items.label: Younger speakers
items.body: I looked at younger speakers separately so an overall average would not hide where the model had more trouble.

items.label: Preschool adaptation
items.body: I also tried adapting the recognizer to preschool speech. The small test group makes this an early result that needs more testing.

items.label: Keeping repetitions and fillers
items.body: I checked which marked repetitions and fillers remained in the transcript. The rules for counting them matter when comparing models.

items.label: Research artifact
items.body: The paper, “SpeakWise: Repair-Ready Child Speech Recognition via Verbatim Evidence Preservation,” describes the study. The full methods are needed to make sense of any reported scores.

2.intro: I still need to test how the new recognizer works with the editing and voice-synthesis stages.
items: Validate repair against the preserved original transcript and audio.
Evaluate synthesis fidelity separately from transcription accuracy.
Measure streaming behavior and latency under specified conditions.
Test how users inspect and control proposed revisions.

paragraphs: I began by asking what I could change in someone’s speech. Showing the prototype to the people who inspired it taught me to ask what they wanted first.

That lesson shaped Phase 2: a recognizer should preserve a detail before anyone decides whether to edit it. I want to keep studying how language carries meaning and how technical choices affect the record we keep of someone’s voice.

pomelo-labs.title: PomeloLabs.ai — AI Search Analytics & Optimization Platform
subtitles: A subscription-based AI marketing platform used by businesses
Founder & Lead Developer · GEO Analytics · Patent Pending

Product Experience & Core User Journey.heading: A Live Product Built for Real Marketing Work

paragraphs: I independently developed PomeloLabs.ai, a live commercial AI marketing platform with active business users on subscriptions. It measures brand visibility across major AI search engines and connects the findings to marketing tasks and content.
For one B2B client, AI discovery rate increased from 21% to 63% (reported October 2026). This is one client’s result, not an average across customers.

I built the architecture, integrations, testing, and deployment. My mother’s company, CrestPoint Marketing, handles marketing and deployed the platform at OneSource Cloud, an existing CrestPoint client. Her business requirements and agency feedback informed the product.

vla-robot-manipulation.title: VLA Robotics — Learning Robot Manipulation with Vision-Language-Action Models
subtitles: Training and evaluating robot manipulation policies across tabletop and lightbox environments
Research Team Leader · UT Dallas STEM Bridge Program · 3rd Place of 20+ Teams

Motivation & Research Value.heading: Researching Robot Learning at UT Dallas

paragraphs: At the six-week UT Dallas STEM Bridge program, I led a five-person team researching vision-language-action models for robotic arms with graduate mentors and faculty at the Intelligent Robotics and Vision Lab.

I helped coordinate data collection, model training, and testing, then worked with the team on our poster, presentation, and live robot demonstration. We placed 3rd of 20+ teams. The experiments and hardware work were shared.
0.title: My Role in a Collaborative Study

paragraphs: The project looked at how a robot uses a camera image and an instruction to choose an action. One example was picking up bread and placing it on a red plate.
We compared how policies worked in tabletop and lightbox settings, including what happened when the training environment and test environment were different.
A demonstration includes more than the motion we want the robot to learn. It also includes the background and lighting. Changing the scene helped us ask which details the policy was relying on.
2.title: Why the Data Distribution Matters

Data Collection & Model Training.heading: Collecting Data and Training the Policy

paragraphs: We used a leader arm to guide a follower arm and recorded what the camera saw alongside the arm’s actions. We then trained SmolVLA and tested it on the real arm. As team leader, I helped coordinate the steps and keep the experiment moving.

The poster compares pretrained π0.5 and SmolVLA policies on VLARePlica tasks. We then used SmolVLA for the tabletop and lightbox experiments. These comparisons describe our particular tasks and test conditions.

1.title: Policy Comparison — Read With the Poster Protocol

items.label: π0.5
items.body: The reported comparison favored this policy under the poster’s specific conditions, not across robotics settings generally.

items.label: SmolVLA
items.body: The team selected this policy for further experiments within available resources. Model choice and environment transfer are separate questions.

paragraphs: For one task, the robot had to pick up bread and put it on a red plate. We compared policies trained with tabletop demonstrations, lightbox demonstrations, and a mixture of both. The poster gives the trial setup needed to interpret the results.
2.title: A Fixed Task Under Different Conditions

items.label: Tabletop → Tabletop
items.body: The poster reports stronger performance when training and execution matched.

items.label: Tabletop → Lightbox
items.body: Moving to a different scene reduced success in the reported runs.

items.label: Merged → Tabletop
items.body: Combining demonstrations improved the observed cross-condition behavior.

items.label: Merged → Lightbox
items.body: Mixed-condition training also improved behavior in the lightbox relative to single-condition transfer.

items.label: Lightbox → Tabletop
items.body: The reverse transfer exposed a similar sensitivity to scene changes.

items.label: Lightbox → Lightbox
items.body: Success in a matching environment did not establish robustness outside it.

items.label: Matching conditions can conceal brittleness
items.body: Doing well in the training setup does not tell us enough about how a policy will do somewhere else.

items.label: Data diversity is a useful intervention
items.body: Using demonstrations from both conditions helped in our tests. I would want more experiments before drawing a broader conclusion.

items.label: Other explanations remain possible
items.body: We changed several scene details at once. Further tests could separate the effects of lighting and background.

paragraphs: I helped keep the work connected from demonstrations through training and testing, and helped the team present what we found. The results reflect our shared experiments and our mentors’ guidance.

items.label: Evaluation

paragraphs: A robot could do well where it trained and struggle after the scene changed. Comparing tabletop and lightbox settings taught me to examine what the training examples contained, including lighting and background.
Leading the team meant coordinating experiments and explaining the results with my teammates. I learned to keep each conclusion tied to the task and conditions we actually tested.

expressive.title: Expressive — Open-Source Audio Plugin
subtitles: An open-source audio plugin I built with C++ and JUCE
Independent Developer · C++ / JUCE · Open Source

Motivation.heading: From Making Music to Making a Plugin

paragraphs: I independently built Expressive in C++ with JUCE, inspired by my own music production and experience playing piano and clarinet. The VST3 effect maps MIDI note velocity to stereo movement.
Reported October 2026: 3,400+ downloads from producers and 40+ GitHub stars. I released the code as open source so others could use and change it.

items.title: Read the performance input
items.body: A MIDI note-on message includes a velocity value. The plugin maps that value to a position between left and right.

items.title: Smooth the transition
items.body: The sound moves toward the new position over a chosen interval, which helps avoid abrupt jumps and clicks.

items.title: Render the spatial change
items.body: Equal-power panning sets the left and right levels. I also added a choice between working from a mono sum and balancing the existing stereo signal.

1.title: Controls as Choices About the Mapping

items.title: Smoothing Time
items.body: How quickly should a change in playing dynamics become a change in stereo position?

items.title: Pan Width
items.body: How strongly should velocity affect movement? A narrower range keeps the effect subtler.

items.title: Pan Curve
items.body: How should velocity differences be distributed across stereo space?

items.title: Mono Collapse
items.body: Should the tool reposition a mono sum or preserve more of the existing stereo relationship?

1.title: From a Music Idea to a Release
items: I built the effect and controls, packaged the plugin, and released the source code.
The October 2026 snapshot records 3,400+ downloads from producers and 40+ GitHub stars.
Listening while adjusting the smoothing, width, and curve helped me connect a control’s behavior to what another musician would hear.
I learned to build within existing music software. The standalone version also lets someone try the effect without a digital audio workstation.

items.label: Making it understandable
items.body: Can I explain a difficult idea clearly while keeping the important assumptions visible?

paragraphs: I built the workflow from API data to an interactive explanation. The 1,000+ Google Search Console clicks reported by October 2026 show that people found the site through search; evaluating how well they understood it is a separate next step.
2.title: My Contribution and the Site’s Reach

paragraphs: Connecting external data, calculations, and AI responses taught me to check each stage separately. A clear sentence can still describe the wrong number.
I became more interested in how people read unfamiliar information. I want to build explanations that help a reader check the source and ask a better follow-up question.

elocutionist.title: Elocutionist — Speaking & Interview Practice
subtitles: Interview practice with AI questions and feedback

paragraphs: I independently built Elocutionist to connect background documents, generated questions, typed or spoken answers, and AI feedback in one practice session. My work included document processing, Whisper transcription, and feedback about content and structure.
This is separate from the team-built module at DreamCollege.ai. Its feedback supports practice, not an admissions judgment.

items.title: Add background
items.body: The app reads background information and document text to create relevant questions.

items.title: Capture a response
items.body: Users type or record an answer. Whisper turns the recording into text for the feedback step.

items.title: Generate feedback
items.body: The model returns suggestions about the answer’s content and structure. Users decide which suggestions fit.

items.title: Review and practice again
items.body: Users can play back recordings and revisit earlier answers before trying again.

paragraphs: I added interactive 3D interviewer avatars, drawing inspiration from Proxona, as another way to practice alongside text and voice. I would need user testing to know whether they make practice more effective.
1.title: Trying a 3D Interviewer

Human-AI Interaction Design.heading: Helping the Speaker Stay in Control

items.label: The speaker’s own words
items.body: Give users room to answer in their own words before offering suggestions.

items.label: Relevant questions
items.body: Use the background they provide to ask relevant questions, while allowing for mistakes in reading the documents.

items.label: Specific suggestions
items.body: Explain which part of an answer could be clearer so the speaker can decide whether the suggestion fits.

items.label: Looking back at an answer
items.body: Let users revisit their responses and recordings. Treat the AI score as one piece of feedback.

paragraphs: Connecting document reading, question generation, transcription, and feedback taught me how an error in one step can affect the next. A transcript gives the model words to review, but it misses parts of the speaker’s delivery.

I wanted users to get specific suggestions while deciding how to revise their own answers. Building this independently, then working with a team at DreamCollege.ai, gave me practice in two different development settings.
